templates.title: Equilibria of an autonomous equation and their stability

variants.problem:
Consider the autonomous equation

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2} \left(y + 3\right).\]

(a) Find all equilibrium solutions and classify each as stable, unstable or semistable.
(b) If $y(0)=-4$, what is $\lim_{t\to\infty}y(t)$?
variants.solution:
(a) Equilibria are where $f(y)=y^{2} \left(y + 3\right)=0$: $y=-3$, $y=0$. Test the sign of $f$ between them:

intervaltest $y$sign of $f$$y(t)$ is
$y\lt -3$$-4$$-$decreasing ↓
$-3\lt y\lt 0$$- \frac{3}{2}$$+$increasing ↑
$y>0$$1$$+$increasing ↑

$y=-3$: unstable, since solutions on both sides move away from it.

$y=0$: semistable, since $f$ has the same sign on both sides, so solutions approach from one side and leave on the other.

(b) $f(-4)$ is negative, so $y$ decreases from $-4$ with no equilibrium in the way, so $y(t)\to-\infty$.

variants.problem:
Consider the autonomous equation

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\left(y - 4\right) \left(y - 3\right) \left(y - 1\right).\]

(a) Find all equilibrium solutions and classify each as stable, unstable or semistable.
(b) If $y(0)=\frac{3}{2}$, what is $\lim_{t\to\infty}y(t)$?
variants.solution:
(a) Equilibria are where $f(y)=\left(y - 4\right) \left(y - 3\right) \left(y - 1\right)=0$: $y=1$, $y=3$, $y=4$. Test the sign of $f$ between them:

intervaltest $y$sign of $f$$y(t)$ is
$y\lt 1$$0$$-$decreasing ↓
$1\lt y\lt 3$$2$$+$increasing ↑
$3\lt y\lt 4$$\frac{7}{2}$$-$decreasing ↓
$y>4$$5$$+$increasing ↑

$y=1$: unstable, since solutions on both sides move away from it.

$y=3$: stable, since solutions on both sides move toward it.

$y=4$: unstable, since solutions on both sides move away from it.

(b) $f(\frac{3}{2})$ is positive, so $y$ increases from $\frac{3}{2}$ toward the equilibrium $y=3$, which it never crosses: $\lim_{t\to\infty}y(t)=3$.

templates.title: General solution of a separable equation

variants.problem:
Find the general solution of

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{\cos{\left(3 t \right)}}{2 y - 3}.\]

An implicit solution is fine.
variants.solution:
Separate the variables:

\[\left(2 y - 3\right)dy=\cos{\left(3 t \right)}\,dt.\]

Integrate the left side: $\int\left(2 y - 3\right)dy=y^{2} - 3 y$. For the right side: $\int \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\,dt=\frac{\sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}+C$.

So the general solution is

\[y^{2} - 3 y=\frac{\sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}+C.\]

Check: differentiating implicitly, $\left(2 y - 3\right)y'=\cos{\left(3 t \right)}$, which is the original equation.

variants.problem:
Find the general solution of

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}}{y - 1}.\]

An implicit solution is fine.
variants.solution:
Separate the variables:

\[\left(y - 1\right)dy=2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\,dt.\]

Integrate the left side: $\int\left(y - 1\right)dy=\frac{y^{2}}{2} - y$. For the right side: $\int 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\,dt=\frac{2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}+C$.

So the general solution is

\[\frac{y^{2}}{2} - y=\frac{2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}+C.\]

Check: differentiating implicitly, $\left(y - 1\right)y'=2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}$, which is the original equation.

Integrate the left side: $\int\left(3 y^{2} + 2\right)dy=y^{3} + 2 y$. For the right side: $\int 6 t^{2}\,dt=2 t^{3}+C$.

So the general solution is

\[y^{3} + 2 y=2 t^{3}+C.\]

Check: differentiating implicitly, $\left(3 y^{2} + 2\right)y'=6 t^{2}$, which is the original equation.

variants.problem:

variants.solution:
Separate the variables:

\[\left(2 e^{y}\right)dy=t \cos{\left(t \right)}\,dt.\]

Integrate the left side: $\int\left(2 e^{y}\right)dy=2 e^{y}$. For the right side: By parts with $u=t$, $dv=\cos{\left(t \right)}\,dt$ (so $du=dt$, $v=\sin{\left(t \right)}$): $\int t \cos{\left(t \right)}\,dt=\Big[t \sin{\left(t \right)}-\int \sin{\left(t \right)}\,dt\Big]=t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}+C$.

So the general solution is

\[2 e^{y}=t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}+C.\]

Check: differentiating implicitly, $\left(2 e^{y}\right)y'=t \cos{\left(t \right)}$, which is the original equation.

templates.title: A linear first-order initial value problem (integrating factor)

variants.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

\[y'+\frac{y}{t}=3 t,\qquad y(1)=4,\qquad t>0.\]
variants.solution:
The equation is linear with $p(t)=\frac{1}{t}$. Integrating factor:

\[\mu(t)=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{1\ln t}=t.\]

Multiply through by $\mu$; the left side becomes a product rule:

\[\left(t\,y\right)'=3 t^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ t\,y=t^{3}+C.\]

At $t=1$: $4=1+C$, so $C=3$. Divide by $t$:

\[y=t^{2} + \frac{3}{t}.\]

variants.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

\[y'+4\frac{y}{t}=t^{2},\qquad y(1)=1,\qquad t>0.\]
variants.solution:
The equation is linear with $p(t)=\frac{4}{t}$. Integrating factor:

\[\mu(t)=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{4\ln t}=t^{4}.\]

Multiply through by $\mu$; the left side becomes a product rule:

\[\left(t^{4}\,y\right)'=t^{6}\ \Rightarrow\ t^{4}\,y=\frac{t^{7}}{7}+C.\]

At $t=1$: $1=\frac{1}{7}+C$, so $C=\frac{6}{7}$. Divide by $t^{4}$:

\[y=\frac{t^{3}}{7} + \frac{6}{7 t^{4}}.\]

variants.problem:

variants.solution:
The equation is linear with $p(t)=\frac{2}{t}$. Integrating factor:

\[\mu(t)=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{2\ln t}=t^{2}.\]

Multiply through by $\mu$; the left side becomes a product rule:

\[\left(t^{2}\,y\right)'=2 t^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ t^{2}\,y=\frac{2 t^{3}}{3}+C.\]

At $t=1$: $-2=\frac{2}{3}+C$, so $C=- \frac{8}{3}$. Divide by $t^{2}$:

\[y=\frac{2 t}{3} - \frac{8}{3 t^{2}}.\]

variants.problem:

The equation is linear with $p(t)=- \frac{1}{t}$. Integrating factor:

\[\mu(t)=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{-1\ln t}=\frac{1}{t}.\]

Multiply through by $\mu$; the left side becomes a product rule:

\[\left(\frac{1}{t}\,y\right)'=3 t\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{1}{t}\,y=\frac{3 t^{2}}{2}+C.\]

At $t=1$: $2=\frac{3}{2}+C$, so $C=\frac{1}{2}$. Divide by $\frac{1}{t}$:

\[y=\frac{3 t^{3}}{2} + \frac{t}{2}.\]

templates.title: Explicit solution of a separable initial value problem

variants.problem:
Find the explicit solution of the initial value problem

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{3 x}\,y,\qquad y(0)=2.\]
variants.solution:
Separate the variables and integrate:

\[\frac{dy}{y}=e^{3 x}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ \ln|y|=\frac{e^{3 x}}{3}+C\ \Rightarrow\ y=Ae^{\frac{e^{3 x}}{3}}.\]

At $x=0$: $2=Ae^{\frac{1}{3}}$, so $A=\frac{2}{e^{\frac{1}{3}}}$:

\[y=2 e^{\frac{e^{3 x}}{3} - \frac{1}{3}}.\]

Check: $y(0)=2$.

variants.problem:
Find the explicit solution of the initial value problem

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=3 x^{2}\,e^{- y - 1},\qquad y(0)=-1.\]
variants.solution:
Separate the variables and integrate:

\[e^{y + 1}\,dy=3 x^{2}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ e^{y + 1}=x^{3}+C.\]

At $x=0$, $y=-1$: $e^{0}=0+C$, so $C=1$. Take logarithms:

\[y=\ln{\left(x^{3} + 1 \right)} - 1.\]

Check: $y(0)=-1$.

templates.title: An Euler equation: try y = tʳ

variants.problem:
For $t>0$, consider

\[t^2y''-3ty'+3y=0.\]

The coefficients are not constant, so $y=e^{rt}$ will not work. Look for solutions of the form $y=t^r$ and find the general solution.
variants.solution:
With $y=t^r$: $y'=rt^{r-1}$ and $y''=r(r-1)t^{r-2}$, so $t^2y''=r(r-1)t^r$ and $ty'=rt^r$. Substitute and divide by $t^r$:

\[r(r-1)-3r+3=r^{2} - 4 r + 3=(r - 1)(r - 3)=0.\]

The roots are $r=1$ and $r=3$, giving $y_1=t$ and $y_2=t^{3}$.

They are not multiples of each other, so the general solution is

\[y=c_1t+c_2t^{3}.\]

variants.problem:
For $t>0$, consider

\[t^2y''-2ty'-4y=0.\]

The coefficients are not constant, so $y=e^{rt}$ will not work. Look for solutions of the form $y=t^r$ and find the general solution.
variants.solution:
With $y=t^r$: $y'=rt^{r-1}$ and $y''=r(r-1)t^{r-2}$, so $t^2y''=r(r-1)t^r$ and $ty'=rt^r$. Substitute and divide by $t^r$:

\[r(r-1)-2r-4=r^{2} - 3 r - 4=(r + 1)(r - 4)=0.\]

The roots are $r=-1$ and $r=4$, giving $y_1=\frac{1}{t}$ and $y_2=t^{4}$.

They are not multiples of each other, so the general solution is

\[y=c_1\frac{1}{t}+c_2t^{4}.\]

variants.problem:
For $t>0$, consider

\[t^2y''+3ty'+y=0.\]

The coefficients are not constant, so $y=e^{rt}$ will not work. Look for solutions of the form $y=t^r$ and find the general solution.
variants.solution:
With $y=t^r$: $y'=rt^{r-1}$ and $y''=r(r-1)t^{r-2}$, so $t^2y''=r(r-1)t^r$ and $ty'=rt^r$. Substitute and divide by $t^r$:

\[r(r-1)+3r+=r^{2} + 2 r + 1=(r + 1)^2=0.\]

$r=-1$ is a double root. One solution is $y_1=\frac{1}{t}$; for a repeated root of an Euler equation the second is $y_2=\frac{\ln{\left(t \right)}}{t}$.

They are not multiples of each other, so the general solution is

\[y=c_1\frac{1}{t}+c_2\frac{\ln{\left(t \right)}}{t}.\]

The roots are $r=1$ and $r=-1$, giving $y_1=t$ and $y_2=\frac{1}{t}$.

They are not multiples of each other, so the general solution is

\[y=c_1t+c_2\frac{1}{t}.\]

Homogeneous part. The characteristic equation is $r^2-r-12=0$, i.e. $(r + 3)(r - 4)=0$, so $r=-3,\ 4$ and $y_h=c_1e^{- 3 t}+c_2e^{4 t}$.

which gives $A=- \frac{3}{10}$. So $Y=- \frac{3 e^{- t}}{10}$.

\[y=c_1e^{- 3 t}+c_2e^{4 t}- \frac{3 e^{- t}}{10}.\]

templates.title: A damped mass–spring system from physical data

variants.problem:
A weight of $32$ lb stretches a spring $\frac{16}{5}$ ft. The weight moves through a medium that resists with a force of $2$ lb for every ft/s of velocity. It is pulled $\frac{1}{2}$ ft below equilibrium and released. Use $g=32$ ft/s² and take down as positive.

(a) Write the initial value problem for the displacement $u(t)$ (in ft).
(b) Is the motion underdamped, critically damped or overdamped?
(c) Solve for $u(t)$.
variants.solution:
(a) Mass $m=\frac{32}{32}=1$ slug. Spring constant $k=\frac{32}{\frac{16}{5}}=10$ lb/ft. Damping $\gamma=2$ lb·s/ft:

\[u'' + 2u' + 10u=0,\qquad u(0)=\frac{1}{2},\quad u'(0)=0.\]

(b) $\gamma^2-4mk=4-4\left(1\right)(10)=-36$, which is negative: underdamped.

(c) The characteristic equation $r^{2} + 2 r + 10=0$ gives $r=-1\pm 3i$, so $u=\left(C_{1} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + C_{2} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\right) e^{- t}$. From $u(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $u'(0)=0$: $C_1=\frac{1}{2}$, $C_2=\frac{1}{6}$.

\[u(t)=\left(\frac{\sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{6} + \frac{\cos{\left(3 t \right)}}{2}\right) e^{- t}.\]

variants.problem:
A weight of $64$ lb stretches a spring $\frac{8}{5}$ ft. The weight moves through a medium that resists with a force of $18$ lb for every ft/s of velocity. It is pulled $\frac{1}{4}$ ft below equilibrium and released with an initial velocity of $1$ ft/s upward. Use $g=32$ ft/s² and take down as positive.

(a) Write the initial value problem for the displacement $u(t)$ (in ft).
(b) Is the motion underdamped, critically damped or overdamped?
(c) Solve for $u(t)$.
variants.solution:
(a) Mass $m=\frac{64}{32}=2$ slug. Spring constant $k=\frac{64}{\frac{8}{5}}=40$ lb/ft. Damping $\gamma=18$ lb·s/ft:

\[2u'' + 18u' + 40u=0,\qquad u(0)=\frac{1}{4},\quad u'(0)=-1.\]

(b) $\gamma^2-4mk=324-4\left(2\right)(40)=4$, which is positive: overdamped.

(c) The characteristic equation $2 r^{2} + 18 r + 40=0$ gives $r=-5,\ -4$, so $u=C_{1} e^{- 5 t} + C_{2} e^{- 4 t}$. From $u(0)=\frac{1}{4}$ and $u'(0)=-1$: $C_1=0$, $C_2=\frac{1}{4}$.

\[u(t)=\frac{e^{- 4 t}}{4}.\]

variants.problem:
A weight of $16$ lb stretches a spring $\frac{32}{9}$ ft. The weight moves through a medium that resists with a force of $3$ lb for every ft/s of velocity. It is pulled $1$ ft below equilibrium and released. Use $g=32$ ft/s² and take down as positive.

(a) Write the initial value problem for the displacement $u(t)$ (in ft).
(b) Is the motion underdamped, critically damped or overdamped?
(c) Solve for $u(t)$.
variants.solution:
(a) Mass $m=\frac{16}{32}=\frac{1}{2}$ slug. Spring constant $k=\frac{16}{\frac{32}{9}}=\frac{9}{2}$ lb/ft. Damping $\gamma=3$ lb·s/ft:

\[\frac{1}{2}u'' + 3u' + \frac{9}{2}u=0,\qquad u(0)=1,\quad u'(0)=0.\]

(b) $\gamma^2-4mk=9-4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(\frac{9}{2})=0$, which is zero: critically damped.

(c) The characteristic equation $\frac{r^{2}}{2} + 3 r + \frac{9}{2}=0$ gives $r=-3\ \text{(double root)}$, so $u=\left(C_{1} + C_{2} t\right) e^{- 3 t}$. From $u(0)=1$ and $u'(0)=0$: $C_1=1$, $C_2=3$.

\[u(t)=\left(3 t + 1\right) e^{- 3 t}.\]

variants.problem:

(b) Is the motion underdamped, critically damped or overdamped?
(c) Solve for $u(t)$.
variants.solution:
(a) Mass $m=\frac{64}{32}=2$ slug. Spring constant $k=\frac{64}{8}=8$ lb/ft. Damping $\gamma=10$ lb·s/ft:

\[2u'' + 10u' + 8u=0,\qquad u(0)=\frac{1}{2},\quad u'(0)=-1.\]

(b) $\gamma^2-4mk=100-4\left(2\right)(8)=36$, which is positive: overdamped.

(c) The characteristic equation $2 r^{2} + 10 r + 8=0$ gives $r=-4,\ -1$, so $u=C_{1} e^{- 4 t} + C_{2} e^{- t}$. From $u(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $u'(0)=-1$: $C_1=\frac{1}{6}$, $C_2=\frac{1}{3}$.

\[u(t)=\frac{e^{- t}}{3} + \frac{e^{- 4 t}}{6}.\]

\[u'' + 5u' + 4u=0,\qquad u(0)=\frac{1}{2},\quad u'(0)=2.\]

(b) $\gamma^2-4mk=25-4\left(1\right)(4)=9$, which is positive: overdamped.

(c) The characteristic equation $r^{2} + 5 r + 4=0$ gives $r=-4,\ -1$, so $u=C_{1} e^{- 4 t} + C_{2} e^{- t}$. From $u(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $u'(0)=2$: $C_1=- \frac{5}{6}$, $C_2=\frac{4}{3}$.

\[u(t)=\frac{4 e^{- t}}{3} - \frac{5 e^{- 4 t}}{6}.\]

templates.title: Steady-state response of a forced, damped spring

variants.problem:
A spring–mass system with $m=1$ satisfies

\[y'' + y' + y=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

(a) Find the steady-state solution (the part that does not die out).
(b) What is its amplitude?
variants.solution:
(a) Damping makes the homogeneous solutions decay, so the steady state is the particular solution $Y=A\cos 1t+B\sin 1t$. Then $Y'=-1A\sin 1t+1B\cos 1t$ and $Y''=-1Y$. Substituting and matching the $\cos 1t$ and $\sin 1t$ terms:

\[\begin{aligned}\cos 1t:&\quad B=2\\ \sin 1t:&\quad - A=0\end{aligned}\]

Solving: $A=0$, $B=2$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=2 \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

(b) Amplitude $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}=2$.

variants.problem:
A spring–mass system with $m=1$ satisfies

\[y'' + 4y' + 9y=2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

(a) Find the steady-state solution (the part that does not die out).
(b) What is its amplitude?
variants.solution:
(a) Damping makes the homogeneous solutions decay, so the steady state is the particular solution $Y=A\cos 3t+B\sin 3t$. Then $Y'=-3A\sin 3t+3B\cos 3t$ and $Y''=-9Y$. Substituting and matching the $\cos 3t$ and $\sin 3t$ terms:

\[\begin{aligned}\cos 3t:&\quad 12 B=2\\ \sin 3t:&\quad - 12 A=2\end{aligned}\]

Solving: $A=- \frac{1}{6}$, $B=\frac{1}{6}$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=\frac{\sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{6} - \frac{\cos{\left(3 t \right)}}{6}.\]

(b) Amplitude $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}$.

(b) What is its amplitude?
variants.solution:

\[\begin{aligned}\cos 1t:&\quad 8 A + B=1\\ \sin 1t:&\quad - A + 8 B=-2\end{aligned}\]

Solving: $A=\frac{2}{13}$, $B=- \frac{3}{13}$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=- \frac{3 \sin{\left(t \right)}}{13} + \frac{2 \cos{\left(t \right)}}{13}.\]

(a) Damping makes the homogeneous solutions decay, so the steady state is the particular solution $Y=A\cos 2t+B\sin 2t$. Then $Y'=-2A\sin 2t+2B\cos 2t$ and $Y''=-4Y$. Substituting and matching the $\cos 2t$ and $\sin 2t$ terms:

Solving: $A=\frac{5}{89}$, $B=\frac{8}{89}$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=\frac{8 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{89} + \frac{5 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}}{89}.\]

\[y'' + 4y' + 9y=- \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

(a) Find the steady-state solution (the part that does not die out).
(b) What is its amplitude?
variants.solution:
(a) Damping makes the homogeneous solutions decay, so the steady state is the particular solution $Y=A\cos 2t+B\sin 2t$. Then $Y'=-2A\sin 2t+2B\cos 2t$ and $Y''=-4Y$. Substituting and matching the $\cos 2t$ and $\sin 2t$ terms:

\[\begin{aligned}\cos 2t:&\quad 5 A + 8 B=-4\\ \sin 2t:&\quad - 8 A + 5 B=-1\end{aligned}\]

Solving: $A=- \frac{12}{89}$, $B=- \frac{37}{89}$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=- \frac{37 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{89} - \frac{12 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}}{89}.\]

(b) Amplitude $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}=\frac{\sqrt{1513}}{89}$.

variants.problem:

\[y'' + 3y' + 4y=- 2 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

(a) Find the steady-state solution (the part that does not die out).
(b) What is its amplitude?
variants.solution:
(a) Damping makes the homogeneous solutions decay, so the steady state is the particular solution $Y=A\cos 2t+B\sin 2t$. Then $Y'=-2A\sin 2t+2B\cos 2t$ and $Y''=-4Y$. Substituting and matching the $\cos 2t$ and $\sin 2t$ terms:

\[\begin{aligned}\cos 2t:&\quad 6 B=1\\ \sin 2t:&\quad - 6 A=-2\end{aligned}\]

Solving: $A=\frac{1}{3}$, $B=\frac{1}{6}$.

\[y_{ss}(t)=\frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{6} + \frac{\cos{\left(2 t \right)}}{3}.\]

(b) Amplitude $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{6}$.

templates.title: Inverse Laplace transform: partial fractions and completing the square

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}+\frac{s}{s^{2} + 6 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=t - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{2} - \frac{3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}=\frac{1}{2 \left(s + 2\right)} - \frac{1}{2 s} + \frac{1}{s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $t - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{2}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 6 s + 13=(s+3)^2+4$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-3$, $w=2$:

\[\frac{s}{(s+3)^2+4}=\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^2+2^2}-\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+2^2}\ \to\ \left(- \frac{3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{- 3 t}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=t - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{2} - \frac{3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}+\frac{1}{s^{2} + 4 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}=\frac{1}{4 \left(s + 2\right)} - \frac{1}{4 s} + \frac{1}{2 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $\frac{t}{2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{4}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 4 s + 13=(s+2)^2+9$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-2$, $w=3$:

\[\frac{1}{(s+2)^2+9}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{(s+2)^2+3^2}\ \to\ \frac{e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=\frac{t}{2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{4}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s - 1\right)}+\frac{s - 2}{s^{2} - 2 s + 2}\right\}.\]
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s - 1\right)}=\frac{1}{s - 1} - \frac{1}{s} - \frac{1}{s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $- t + e^{t} - 1$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} - 2 s + 2=(s-1)^2+1$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=1$, $w=1$:

\[\frac{s - 2}{(s-1)^2+1}=\frac{s-1}{(s-1)^2+1^2}-1\cdot\frac{1}{(s-1)^2+1^2}\ \to\ \left(- \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) e^{t}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=- t - e^{t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + e^{t} \cos{\left(t \right)} + e^{t} - 1.\]

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{4}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}+\frac{1}{s^{2} + 2 s + 2}\right\}.\]

First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{4}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}=\frac{4}{9 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{4}{9 s} + \frac{4}{3 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $\frac{4 t}{3} - \frac{4}{9} + \frac{4 e^{- 3 t}}{9}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 2 s + 2=(s+1)^2+1$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-1$, $w=1$:

\[\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+1}=1\cdot\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+1^2}\ \to\ e^{- t} \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=\frac{4 t}{3} - \frac{4}{9} + e^{- t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + \frac{4 e^{- 3 t}}{9}.\]

variants.answer: $f(t)=- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4} + e^{- t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s - 2\right)}=\frac{3}{4 \left(s - 2\right)} - \frac{3}{4 s} - \frac{3}{2 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 2 s + 10=(s+1)^2+9$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-1$, $w=3$:

\[\frac{3}{(s+1)^2+9}=1\cdot\frac{3}{(s+1)^2+3^2}\ \to\ e^{- t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4} + e^{- t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s - 2\right)}+\frac{6}{s^{2} + 6 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4} + 3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s - 2\right)}=\frac{3}{4 \left(s - 2\right)} - \frac{3}{4 s} - \frac{3}{2 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 6 s + 13=(s+3)^2+4$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-3$, $w=2$:

\[\frac{6}{(s+3)^2+4}=3\cdot\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+2^2}\ \to\ 3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=- \frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{3 e^{2 t}}{4} - \frac{3}{4} + 3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s - 2\right)}+\frac{s + 6}{s^{2} + 6 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=- t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s - 2\right)}=\frac{1}{2 \left(s - 2\right)} - \frac{1}{2 s} - \frac{1}{s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $- t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2} - \frac{1}{2}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 6 s + 13=(s+3)^2+4$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-3$, $w=2$:

\[\frac{s + 6}{(s+3)^2+4}=\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^2+2^2}+\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+2^2}\ \to\ \left(\frac{3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{- 3 t}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=- t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}+\frac{s + 4}{s^{2} + 6 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=\frac{t}{3} - \frac{1}{9} + \frac{e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{9}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}=\frac{1}{9 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{1}{9 s} + \frac{1}{3 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $\frac{t}{3} - \frac{1}{9} + \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{9}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 6 s + 13=(s+3)^2+4$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-3$, $w=2$:

\[\frac{s + 4}{(s+3)^2+4}=\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^2+2^2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+2^2}\ \to\ \left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{- 3 t}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=\frac{t}{3} - \frac{1}{9} + \frac{e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{9}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s - 3\right)}+\frac{s}{s^{2} + 2 s + 5}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=- \frac{t}{3} + \frac{e^{3 t}}{9} - \frac{1}{9} - \frac{e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{s^{2} \left(s - 3\right)}=\frac{1}{9 \left(s - 3\right)} - \frac{1}{9 s} - \frac{1}{3 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $- \frac{t}{3} + \frac{e^{3 t}}{9} - \frac{1}{9}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 2 s + 5=(s+1)^2+4$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-1$, $w=2$:

\[\frac{s}{(s+1)^2+4}=\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}\ \to\ \left(- \frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{- t}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=- \frac{t}{3} + \frac{e^{3 t}}{9} - \frac{1}{9} - \frac{e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s + 1\right)}+\frac{1}{s^{2} + 2 s + 10}\right\}.\]
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s + 1\right)}=\frac{3}{s + 1} - \frac{3}{s} + \frac{3}{s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $3 t - 3 + 3 e^{- t}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} + 2 s + 10=(s+1)^2+9$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=-1$, $w=3$:

\[\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+9}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{(s+1)^2+3^2}\ \to\ \frac{e^{- t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=3 t - 3 + \frac{e^{- t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3} + 3 e^{- t}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}+\frac{2}{s^{2} - 4 s + 13}\right\}.\]
variants.answer: $f(t)=\frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{2 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3} - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3 e^{- 2 t}}{4}$
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{3}{s^{2} \left(s + 2\right)}=\frac{3}{4 \left(s + 2\right)} - \frac{3}{4 s} + \frac{3}{2 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $\frac{3 t}{2} - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3 e^{- 2 t}}{4}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} - 4 s + 13=(s-2)^2+9$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=2$, $w=3$:

\[\frac{2}{(s-2)^2+9}=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{(s-2)^2+3^2}\ \to\ \frac{2 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=\frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{2 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}}{3} - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3 e^{- 2 t}}{4}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}+\frac{3}{s^{2} - 4 s + 5}\right\}.\]
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 3\right)}=\frac{2}{9 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{2}{9 s} + \frac{2}{3 s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $\frac{2 t}{3} - \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2 e^{- 3 t}}{9}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} - 4 s + 5=(s-2)^2+1$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=2$, $w=1$:

\[\frac{3}{(s-2)^2+1}=3\cdot\frac{1}{(s-2)^2+1^2}\ \to\ 3 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=\frac{2 t}{3} + 3 e^{2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} - \frac{2}{9} + \frac{2 e^{- 3 t}}{9}.\]

variants.problem:
Find

\[\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 1\right)}+\frac{6}{s^{2} - 2 s + 2}\right\}.\]
variants.solution:
First term. Partial fractions:

\[\frac{2}{s^{2} \left(s + 1\right)}=\frac{2}{s + 1} - \frac{2}{s} + \frac{2}{s^{2}},\]

and with $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$, $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{1/(s-a)\}=e^{at}$ this gives $2 t - 2 + 2 e^{- t}$.

Second term. Complete the square: $s^{2} - 2 s + 2=(s-1)^2+1$. Using $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\cos wt\}=\frac{s-c}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ and $\mathcal L\{e^{ct}\sin wt\}=\frac{w}{(s-c)^2+w^2}$ with $c=1$, $w=1$:

\[\frac{6}{(s-1)^2+1}=6\cdot\frac{1}{(s-1)^2+1^2}\ \to\ 6 e^{t} \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Altogether:

\[f(t)=2 t + 6 e^{t} \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 + 2 e^{- t}.\]

templates.title: Solve an initial value problem with Laplace transforms

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 5y' + 6y=3 e^{3 t},\qquad y(0)=1,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y-s+5\left(sY-\right)+6Y=\frac{3}{s - 3}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+5s+6=(s+2)(s+3)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=\frac{s^{2} + 2 s - 12}{\left(s - 3\right) \left(s + 2\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{3}{2 \left(s + 3\right)} + \frac{12}{5 \left(s + 2\right)} + \frac{1}{10 \left(s - 3\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{e^{3 t}}{10} + \frac{12 e^{- 2 t}}{5} - \frac{3 e^{- 3 t}}{2}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 2y' - 3y=- 6 e^{2 t},\qquad y(0)=-1,\quad y'(0)=-3.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+s+3+2\left(sY+\right)-3Y=- \frac{6}{s - 2}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+2s-3=(s+3)(s-1)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{s + 4}{\left(s - 2\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=\frac{1}{5 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{6}{5 \left(s - 2\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{6 e^{2 t}}{5} + \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{5}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - 2y' - 3y=3 e^{2 t},\qquad y(0)=-1,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+s-2\left(sY+\right)-3Y=\frac{3}{s - 2}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-2s-3=(s+1)(s-3)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{s^{2} - 4 s + 1}{\left(s - 3\right) \left(s - 2\right) \left(s + 1\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{1}{2 \left(s + 1\right)} - \frac{1}{s - 2} + \frac{1}{2 \left(s - 3\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{e^{3 t}}{2} - e^{2 t} - \frac{e^{- t}}{2}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - y=- 5 e^{- 3 t},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=-2.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2-Y=- \frac{5}{s + 3}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-=(s-1)(s+1)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 s + 11}{\left(s - 1\right) \left(s + 1\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{5}{8 \left(s + 3\right)} + \frac{9}{4 \left(s + 1\right)} - \frac{13}{8 \left(s - 1\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{13 e^{t}}{8} + \frac{9 e^{- t}}{4} - \frac{5 e^{- 3 t}}{8}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - y' - 2y=- 6 e^{t},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=-2.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2-\left(sY\right)-2Y=- \frac{6}{s - 1}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-s-2=(s+1)(s-2)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 \left(s + 2\right)}{\left(s - 2\right) \left(s - 1\right) \left(s + 1\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{1}{3 \left(s + 1\right)} + \frac{3}{s - 1} - \frac{8}{3 \left(s - 2\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{8 e^{2 t}}{3} + 3 e^{t} - \frac{e^{- t}}{3}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - 2y'=6 e^{- 2 t},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=-1.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+-2\left(sY\right)=\frac{6}{s + 2}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-2s=s(s-2)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{s - 4}{s \left(s - 2\right) \left(s + 2\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=\frac{3}{4 \left(s + 2\right)} + \frac{1}{4 \left(s - 2\right)} - \frac{1}{s}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{e^{2 t}}{4} - 1 + \frac{3 e^{- 2 t}}{4}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 3y'=- 5 e^{3 t},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=-2.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2+3\left(sY\right)=- \frac{5}{s - 3}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+3s=(s+3)s$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 s - 1}{s \left(s - 3\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=\frac{7}{18 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{5}{18 \left(s - 3\right)} - \frac{1}{9 s}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{5 e^{3 t}}{18} - \frac{1}{9} + \frac{7 e^{- 3 t}}{18}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + y' - 2y=- 4 e^{- t},\qquad y(0)=1,\quad y'(0)=2.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y-s-2+\left(sY-\right)-2Y=- \frac{4}{s + 1}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+s-2=(s+2)(s-1)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=\frac{s^{2} + 4 s - 1}{\left(s - 1\right) \left(s + 1\right) \left(s + 2\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{5}{3 \left(s + 2\right)} + \frac{2}{s + 1} + \frac{2}{3 \left(s - 1\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{2 e^{t}}{3} + 2 e^{- t} - \frac{5 e^{- 2 t}}{3}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 3y'=- 5 e^{3 t},\qquad y(0)=-2,\quad y'(0)=2.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2s-2+3\left(sY+2\right)=- \frac{5}{s - 3}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+3s=(s+3)s$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 s^{2} - 2 s - 7}{s \left(s - 3\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{17}{18 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{5}{18 \left(s - 3\right)} - \frac{7}{9 s}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{5 e^{3 t}}{18} - \frac{7}{9} - \frac{17 e^{- 3 t}}{18}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 2y'=- 3 e^{3 t},\qquad y(0)=-1,\quad y'(0)=3.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+s-3+2\left(sY+\right)=- \frac{3}{s - 3}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+2s=(s+2)s$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{s^{2} - 4 s + 6}{s \left(s - 3\right) \left(s + 2\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{9}{5 \left(s + 2\right)} - \frac{1}{5 \left(s - 3\right)} + \frac{1}{s}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=- \frac{e^{3 t}}{5} + 1 - \frac{9 e^{- 2 t}}{5}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 4y' + 3y=3 e^{2 t},\qquad y(0)=-2,\quad y'(0)=3.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2s-3+4\left(sY+2\right)+3Y=\frac{3}{s - 2}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+4s+3=(s+1)(s+3)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 s^{2} + s - 13}{\left(s - 2\right) \left(s + 1\right) \left(s + 3\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{1}{5 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{2}{s + 1} + \frac{1}{5 \left(s - 2\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{e^{2 t}}{5} - 2 e^{- t} - \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{5}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - 2y'=3 e^{- t},\qquad y(0)=-2,\quad y'(0)=-1.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+2s+-2\left(sY+2\right)=\frac{3}{s + 1}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-2s=s(s-2)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{2 s + 3}{s \left(s + 1\right)}.\]

Partial fractions:

\[Y(s)=\frac{1}{s + 1} - \frac{3}{s}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=-3 + e^{- t}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' - y' - 2y=6,\qquad y(0)=-1,\quad y'(0)=-3.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y+s+3-\left(sY+\right)-2Y=\frac{6}{s}.\]

variants.problem:
Use the Laplace transform to solve

\[y'' + 3y' + 2y=e^{t},\qquad y(0)=1,\quad y'(0)=-3.\]
variants.solution:
Transform both sides, using $\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$ and $\mathcal L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$:

\[s^2Y-s+3+3\left(sY-\right)+2Y=\frac{1}{s - 1}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2+3s+2=(s+1)(s+2)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=\frac{s^{2} - s + 1}{\left(s - 1\right) \left(s + 1\right) \left(s + 2\right)}.\]

\[Y(s)=\frac{7}{3 \left(s + 2\right)} - \frac{3}{2 \left(s + 1\right)} + \frac{1}{6 \left(s - 1\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y(t)=\frac{e^{t}}{6} - \frac{3 e^{- t}}{2} + \frac{7 e^{- 2 t}}{3}.\]

variants.problem:

\[s^2Y+s-3-\left(sY+\right)-2Y=- \frac{4}{s + 2}.\]

Collect the $Y$ terms; note $s^2-s-2=(s-2)(s+1)$. Solving for $Y$:

\[Y(s)=- \frac{s^{2} - 2 s - 4}{\left(s - 2\right) \left(s + 1\right) \left(s + 2\right)}.\]

\[Y(s)=- \frac{1}{s + 2} - \frac{1}{3 \left(s + 1\right)} + \frac{1}{3 \left(s - 2\right)}.\]

Invert each term with $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{1}{s-a}\right\}=e^{at}$:

\[y'' + y' - 2y=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<3\\ 1, & t\ge 3\end{cases},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.solution:
Write the forcing with a unit step function: $g(t)=1u_{3}(t)$, so $\mathcal L\{g\}=\frac{1e^{-3s}}{s}$.

With zero initial conditions, transforming gives $\left(s^2+s-2\right)Y=\mathcal L\{g\}$, so

\[Y(s)=1e^{-3s}H(s),\qquad H(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+2)(s-1)}.\]

Partial fractions and inversion of $H$:

\[H(s)=\frac{1}{6 \left(s + 2\right)} + \frac{1}{3 \left(s - 1\right)} - \frac{1}{2 s}\ \Rightarrow\ h(t)=\frac{e^{t}}{3} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{- 2 t}}{6}.\]

A factor $e^{-3s}$ shifts: $\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-3s}H(s)\}=u_{3}(t)\,h(t-3)$. So $y(t)=1u_{3}(t)\,h(t-3)$, i.e.

\[y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<3\\ \frac{e^{t}}{3 e^{3}} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{6} e^{- 2 t}}{6}, & t\ge 3\end{cases}\]

\[y'' - 2y' - 3y=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<3\\ 3, & t\ge 3\end{cases},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.answer: \[y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<3\\ \frac{e^{3 t}}{4 e^{9}} - 1 + \frac{3 e^{3} e^{- t}}{4}, & t\ge 3\end{cases}\]
variants.solution:

Partial fractions and inversion of $H$:

\[H(s)=\frac{1}{4 \left(s + 1\right)} + \frac{1}{12 \left(s - 3\right)} - \frac{1}{3 s}\ \Rightarrow\ h(t)=\frac{e^{3 t}}{12} - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{e^{- t}}{4}.\]

A factor $e^{-3s}$ shifts: $\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-3s}H(s)\}=u_{3}(t)\,h(t-3)$. So $y(t)=3u_{3}(t)\,h(t-3)$, i.e.

\[y'' + 4y' + 3y=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<1\\ 3, & t\ge 1\end{cases},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.answer: \[y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & 0\le t<1\\ 1 - \frac{3 e e^{- t}}{2} + \frac{e^{3} e^{- 3 t}}{2}, & t\ge 1\end{cases}\]
variants.solution:
Write the forcing with a unit step function: $g(t)=3u_{1}(t)$, so $\mathcal L\{g\}=\frac{3e^{-1s}}{s}$.

With zero initial conditions, transforming gives $\left(s^2+4s+3\right)Y=\mathcal L\{g\}$, so

\[Y(s)=3e^{-1s}H(s),\qquad H(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+3)(s+1)}.\]

Partial fractions and inversion of $H$:

\[H(s)=\frac{1}{6 \left(s + 3\right)} - \frac{1}{2 \left(s + 1\right)} + \frac{1}{3 s}\ \Rightarrow\ h(t)=\frac{1}{3} - \frac{e^{- t}}{2} + \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{6}.\]

A factor $e^{-1s}$ shifts: $\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-1s}H(s)\}=u_{1}(t)\,h(t-1)$. So $y(t)=3u_{1}(t)\,h(t-1)$, i.e.

variants.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

\[y'' - 3y' + 2y=\begin{cases}4, & 0\le t<1\\ 0, & t\ge 1\end{cases},\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=0.\]
variants.solution:
Write the forcing with a unit step function: $g(t)=4\big(1-u_{1}(t)\big)$, so $\mathcal L\{g\}=\frac{4\left(1-e^{-1s}\right)}{s}$.

With zero initial conditions, transforming gives $\left(s^2-3s+2\right)Y=\mathcal L\{g\}$, so

\[Y(s)=4\big(1-e^{-1s}\big)H(s),\qquad H(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-2)(s-1)}.\]

Partial fractions and inversion of $H$:

\[H(s)=- \frac{1}{s - 1} + \frac{1}{2 \left(s - 2\right)} + \frac{1}{2 s}\ \Rightarrow\ h(t)=\frac{e^{2 t}}{2} - e^{t} + \frac{1}{2}.\]

A factor $e^{-1s}$ shifts: $\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-1s}H(s)\}=u_{1}(t)\,h(t-1)$. So $y(t)=4\big[h(t)-u_{1}(t)\,h(t-1)\big]$, i.e.

\[y(t)=\begin{cases}2 e^{2 t} - 4 e^{t} + 2, & 0\le t<1\\ - \frac{2 e^{2 t}}{e^{2}} + 2 e^{2 t} - 4 e^{t} + \frac{4 e^{t}}{e}, & t\ge 1\end{cases}\]

templates.title: A linear model with exponential forcing (integrating factor)

variants.problem:
The temperature $T(t)$ (°C) of an object satisfies

\[T'+\frac{1}{4}T=\frac{15}{2}+80e^{- \frac{t}{2}},\qquad T(0)=200.\]

(a) Solve for $T(t)$.
(b) What temperature does the object approach in the long run?
variants.solution:
(a) Integrating factor $\mu=e^{\frac{t}{4}}$:

\[\big(Te^{\frac{t}{4}}\big)'=\frac{15}{2}e^{\frac{t}{4}}+80e^{- \frac{t}{4}}\ \Rightarrow\ Te^{\frac{t}{4}}=30e^{\frac{t}{4}}-320e^{- \frac{t}{4}}+C.\]

Divide by $e^{\frac{t}{4}}$: $T=30-320e^{- \frac{t}{2}}+Ce^{- \frac{t}{4}}$. At $t=0$: $200=-290+C$, so $C=490$:

\[T(t)=30 - 320 e^{- \frac{t}{2}} + 490 e^{- \frac{t}{4}}.\]

(b) Both exponentials decay, so $T(t)\to 30$ °C.

templates.title: A mixing tank that is filling up

variants.problem:
A tank holds $200$ L of water containing $0$ g of salt. Brine with $5$ g/L of salt flows in at $4$ L/min, and the well-mixed solution drains out at $2$ L/min. The tank holds $600$ L.

(a) Write an initial value problem for the amount of salt $y(t)$ (g) after $t$ minutes.
(b) Solve it.
(c) How much salt is in the tank when it is full?
variants.solution:
(a) The volume grows by $4-2=2$ L/min, so $V(t)=200+2t$. Salt enters at $4\cdot5=20$ g/min and leaves at $2\cdot\dfrac{y}{200+2t}$ g/min:

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=20-\frac{2y}{200+2t},\qquad y(0)=0.\]

(b) This is linear with $p(t)=\frac{2}{200+2t}$, so $\mu=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{\ln(200+2t)}=(200+2t)$:

\[\Big((200+2t)\,y\Big)'=20(200+2t)\ \Rightarrow\ (200+2t)\,y=\frac{20}{4}(200+2t)^{2}+C.\]

At $t=0$: $200\cdot0=5\cdot200^{2}+C$, so $C=-200000$. Divide by $\mu$:

\[y(t)=5(200+2t)-\frac{200000}{200+2t}.\]

(c) The tank is full when $200+2t=600$, at $t=200$ min. Then

\[y(200)=5\cdot600-\frac{200000}{600}\approx 2666.67\ \text{g}.\]

(b) This is linear with $p(t)=\frac{20}{200+10t}$, so $\mu=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{2\ln(200+10t)}=(200+10t)^{2}$:

At $t=0$: $200^2\cdot20=1\cdot200^{3}+C$, so $C=-7200000$. Divide by $\mu$:

(c) The tank is full when $200+10t=400$, at $t=20$ min. Then

(b) This is linear with $p(t)=\frac{10}{200+10t}$, so $\mu=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{\ln(200+10t)}=(200+10t)$:

\[\Big((200+10t)\,y\Big)'=100(200+10t)\ \Rightarrow\ (200+10t)\,y=\frac{100}{20}(200+10t)^{2}+C.\]

At $t=0$: $200\cdot0=5\cdot200^{2}+C$, so $C=-200000$. Divide by $\mu$:

\[y(t)=5(200+10t)-\frac{200000}{200+10t}.\]

(c) The tank is full when $200+10t=600$, at $t=40$ min. Then

\[y(40)=5\cdot600-\frac{200000}{600}\approx 2666.67\ \text{g}.\]

variants.problem:
A tank holds $200$ L of water containing $50$ g of salt. Brine with $3$ g/L of salt flows in at $15$ L/min, and the well-mixed solution drains out at $10$ L/min. The tank holds $400$ L.

(a) Write an initial value problem for the amount of salt $y(t)$ (g) after $t$ minutes.
(b) Solve it.
(c) How much salt is in the tank when it is full?
variants.solution:
(a) The volume grows by $15-10=5$ L/min, so $V(t)=200+5t$. Salt enters at $15\cdot3=45$ g/min and leaves at $10\cdot\dfrac{y}{200+5t}$ g/min:

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=45-\frac{10y}{200+5t},\qquad y(0)=50.\]

(b) This is linear with $p(t)=\frac{10}{200+5t}$, so $\mu=e^{\int p\,dt}=e^{2\ln(200+5t)}=(200+5t)^{2}$:

\[\Big((200+5t)^{2}\,y\Big)'=45(200+5t)^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ (200+5t)^{2}\,y=\frac{45}{15}(200+5t)^{3}+C.\]

At $t=0$: $200^2\cdot50=3\cdot200^{3}+C$, so $C=-22000000$. Divide by $\mu$:

\[y(t)=3(200+5t)-\frac{22000000}{(200+5t)^{2}}.\]

(c) The tank is full when $200+5t=400$, at $t=40$ min. Then

\[y(40)=3\cdot400-\frac{22000000}{400^2}\approx 1062.50\ \text{g}.\]
